This paper examines the high-temperature transport mechanism in a specific armchair single-wall carbon nanotube film. The experiment involves detailed resistance measurements across different directions and temperatures, ranging from 300 to 450 Kelvin. The results show a carbon nanotube network that exhibits anisotropic electrical conductivity. The calculated electronic band structure aligns with both the theoretical Mexican hat model and an angular-dependent susceptibility model for high-temperature carbon nanotubes. The observed properties can't be fully explained by a carbon nanotube bundle, indicating a crucial role of individual carbon nanotube interactions in the film. The conclusions provide a basis for understanding the transport physics in a carbon nanotube film and identify the carbon nanotube interaction as the dominant high-temperature transport mechanism.

A novel fuzzy k-means clustering method is proposed that addresses several shortcomings in existing approaches. These shortcomings include overemphasizing data outliers observed by the algorithm, resulting in inconsistent clustering results with respect to different initializations. To mitigate this problem, a modified fuzzy k-means method incorporating entropy terms has been introduced as its objective function. Specifically, the objective function is reformulated as the weighted sum of two components, where the first component seeks to minimize the distance between data points and their assigned cluster centroids, and the second component promotes the dispersion among data points assigned to distinct clusters. This modified objective function serves as the basis for a Lagrange multiplier-based iterative optimization framework. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed method in generating membership profiles that adhere to specified constraints, several benchmark datasets have been employed for evaluation. The results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses alternative algorithms in producing accurate and consistent membership profiles.

This research introduces a novel algorithm designed to estimate expert models in complex data sets by leveraging the capabilities of deep neural networks, specifically those with multiple outputs and complex internal structures. The proposed method generates synthetic data samples through a two-step process involving (1) determining optimal distributions for each expert, (2) assigning mixture weights to combine expert predictions. By integrating a normalizing flow model, the algorithm overcomes issues related to vanishing gradients during back-propagation, enabling effective training on large data sets. Evaluations using synthetic and real-world data indicate that the algorithm outperforms baseline methods in both accuracy and convergence speed, with notable applications in attribute-based search systems.

The main objective of this note is to provide an overview of the theoretical foundation for Jacobian and Prym varieties, focusing on the principal outcomes from the perspective of algebraic geometry, with an emphasis on the development of the theory in the second half of the 20th century. It is intended to serve as a standalone summary, augmenting the comprehensive treatise on varieties of differentiable functions, initially written by Narasimhan and developed further by Kateb.

We develop a constraint theory based on a metric with singularities and use it to test the degree to which gravity disrupts the internal symmetries of a theory. When applied to Yang-Mills and N=2 Super Yang-Mills theories, our results show that these theories can maintain their global symmetries intact in specific cases where the space-time geometry has either zero or one singular point. Additionally, for theories of quantum gravity combining these matter theories, our results yield the conclusion that breaking global symmetries may be restricted to 11 and 11 dimensions respectively in specific cases. This implies strict limitations on breaking global symmetries may be imposed by quantum gravity.

To explore subgiant, red giant, and blue horizontal branch star populations, researchers developed stellar models for the omega Centauri globular cluster, taking into account its metal-rich composition. Next, they obtained photometric data transits for about 620 stars that are consistent with those of field stars, allowing them to determine the cluster's age, radius, surface gravity, and metal abundance using _TELESCOPE$_. Their findings indicated that the cluster resides approximately 15.6 kpc away from the Earth. By applying the SAR ($V-J$) color index to determine the star's surface gravity, and using full spectral synthesis to calculate surface gravity, the team discovered that the obtained gravities match the results. They created luminosity diagrams for the star populations and discovered the existence of at least five distinct blue horizontal branch star groups within the cluster, as well as distinguishing differences between first and second generation stars. By applying the Strömgren uvbyβ photometry to calculate the star's flux, the team discovered the existence of multiple stellar populations that are concentrated in the cluster's core, and are believed to be the result of binary coalescence and accretion of smaller globular clusters.

We explore an extension of the Madsen-Weiss theorem to MQ-relations, specifically of the type declared by Morita, which have their roots in multiple quantum invariants that appear in the study of 3-manifolds and their surjections onto surface group manifolds. This extended theorem aligns with the principles of the b-principle and is complemented by a stability variant. The novel idea here is the use of string topology methods initially developed by the MOOP group. An analogous variant for Heegaard Floer coefficients is proposed; note that we don't have a topological manifestation for these coefficients yet.

A deep neural network's ability to generalize effectively heavily relies on the representation learned in the early stages, with the first few layers acquiring basic image characteristics that prove to be highly transferable across different tasks. In stark contrast, the final layers of a well-trained network, specifically the penultimate layer, fail to exhibit significant transferability due to their specialty in producing class-specific features that become specialized and noisy due to overfitting. Given the crucial role of the penultimate layer in producing interpretable features, replacing it with a new layer that is adaptable and capable of learning robust, semantic features is essential. In our work, we utilize meta-learning in the form of Differentiable Neural Architectures Search (DNAS) to discover a customizable penultimate layer that is capable of enhancing the transferability of features across various image classification tasks. In line with the findings of Zhang et al., we utilize a multi-task learning setting where three tasks are simultaneously learned: CNN-6->MNIST, CNN-6->CIFAR100, and the traditional single-task CNN-4->CIFAR10. On this setup, we leverage DNAS to introduce a new, learned class (penultimate) layer, which is capable of enhancing the feature transferability. Following this, we conduct an in-depth feature analysis on both the traditional CNN models as well as the one utilizing DNAS to understand the learned features and feature dynamics. We examine the complex issue of influence spreading and network modularity,
focusing on microglial phagocytosis as a reference point. We propose an information
spreading model resembling microglial behavior, where cells are added to the infected
set when in close proximity to already infected cells. The size of the initial seed
influences the spreading pattern, classifying networks based on their modularity. A
generalized model allows for numerical calculations of the spreading pattern's size,
capable of reaching a target value, which is compared to traditional models such as the contact process. The relationship between the modularity, initial seed size, and target value is mapped out,
revealing two critical conditions for influence spreading in networks: having a large
seed or a network designed to achieve a predetermined impact. Additionally, we
investigate network configurations under high seed sizes and initial spreading rates
or target values, identifying conditions that yield maximal outcomes.

We investigate the geometrically informed $X$-Lagrangian mean curvature flow and its modified version, $X^2$-LCF, where $X$ represents an differential vector field. Our study introduces the Lagrangian angle $\theta_L$ and demonstrates that special Lagrangians minimize it; we also show that these Lagrangians are stable under perturbations and remain unchanged under the $X$-LCF. Our findings indicate that the flow equations for both $X$-LCF and $X^2$-LCF are represented by differential equations involving the second fundamental form and the vector field $X$. Notably, the $X^2$-LCF exhibits distinct behavior among mean curvature flows, displaying an analogy with the nonlinear elliptic flows while retaining the flow's uniqueness and short-time stability. Our work culminates in a convergence result for both $X$-LCF and $X^2$-LCF, where the solutions converge towards special Lagrangians as time progresses.

In delay-locked spread-spectrum channels with no amplification, a discrete-time channel model is developed that maintains low computational complexity. This model represents symbolic amplification, initially conceived by Chevillard et al. in PDCP '11, in a simplified way. We discovered that such a model can accurately represent true channels with small error rates, especially for short unamplified links. This model also has an associated measure to assess the model's precision, allowing for an in-depth analysis of its accuracy and its origin. Moreover, we conclude that in cases where the unamplified link is short, a reasonable error limit can be set, thereby enabling the model to approximate non-amplified links with high precision. This approximation simplifies symbolic amplification and facilitates the use of Chevillard et al.'s techniques, ultimately contributing to the development of more efficient channel models.

As critical information systems and networks are increasingly targeted by
attackers, the need for more effective classification and evaluation of
security breaches grows. Despite this, there is still no widely accepted
taxonomy for categorizing problem-space evasion attacks that exploits vulnerabilities.
Our proposed taxonomy categorizes these breaches along three dimensions: the
type of attack launched, the target of the breach, and the intended outcome.

A novel container called Ozy Container has been devised for orchestrating application services to streamline the deployment and management of those services. With a minimalist design, Ozy Container enables straightforward service orchestration similar to systemd, whereas the Ozy Container itself can be managed and orchestrated by a higher-level container, allowing for hierarchical deployment models. As a container specification, Ozy is compatible with existing container runtime engines such as Docker and can run standard Docker commands. Within a container, an Ozy service can operate alongside a Docker daemon, facilitating seamless integration with other containers and enabling the adoption of Ozy Container through existing container workflows. We have developed a demo environment to validate the concept and demonstrate its practical applications.

The reentrant anomalous phase characterized by both chiral and time-reversal invariance is distinct from the conventional Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian phases. Unlike these established topological phases, this reentrant phase loses its topological nature at two separate quantization thresholds. These threshold points mark the beginning of a continuous topological phase change driven by the Chern number. A crucial aspect of the reentrant phase is its ability to host gapless edge modes that arise from the fusion of chiral edge states, separating the C=1 and C=-1 topological regions from the central topological region with C=0. A new type of phase-twisting mechanism is proposed here to explain the reentrant topological phase transition. Unlike the traditional mechanism involving gap generation and annihilation, this new mechanism involves a change in the sign of the mass term, resulting in a mass perturbation that causes a topological phase change. A possible experimental realization of this reentrant topological phase can be achieved in a clay wafer-based quantum Hall device, where the topological phase change can be interpreted as a sign transition in the quantum Hall conductivity measured vertically to the wafer surface.

Research into primordial black hole formation, particularly in high-mass objects, has focused on a specific model called the Thakurta metric. This model features an extraordinary property - its pressure acts in the opposite direction of spatial volume expansion, as predicted by the fundamental laws. However, upon closer examination, this model has been found to suffer from thermodynamic inconsistencies. To rectify this issue, a solution has been proposed that converts the Thakururta model into a more stable and equilibrium-oriented version. Despite this, the Thakurta model's predictions regarding primordial black hole abundance, which were previously deemed unreliable due to thermodynamic inconsistencies, are now surprisingly validated by the new stable model. Consequently, existing constraints on primordial black holes remain relevant and valid.

Young stars surrounded by dusty discs, featuring unusual ring-like structures, offer a rare chance to study how the rings evolve over time. According to theoretical predictions, ring formation is linked to the instability of the disc's gas flow and subsequent self-organizing patterns of density and pressure. This concept has been verified through computer simulations, but the impact of dust accumulation and growth of cores in the rings remains poorly understood. To gain insight into this process, we analyzed the evolution of unstable shearing waves in rings, finding that they cause localized gas pressure and force the core to grow and develop within confined areas of the discs. This process correlates with cosmic ray-driven diffusion of dust and ions, facilitating both static and migrating core growth, ultimately leading to the formation of planet-like objects. Our research reveals the complex, multilevel interactions involved in the evolution of unstable rings and in the long run, it may imply that most stars in the galaxy may have a diminished potential to develop into large planets.

A theory known as learning with unknown correlation structures, initially developed for robust estimation problems, assumed correlation to be unknown and thus required additional statistical parameters. It's discovered this setup is actually an extension of a more fundamental concept called the non-robust learning theory, where correlation is assumed to be known. The robust learning theory was found to be equivalent to the non-robust one when the signal-to-noise ratio is sufficiently high. The robust learning theory, however, unveiled intriguing properties of optimal solutions, revealing a solution could effectively meet the robust risk without the need for estimating all robustness parameters, instead only needing an upper bound of the correlation upper bound. This discovery further indicates that a specific type of loss, called the $\mathfrak{L}_2$ loss, could be effectively minimized without knowledge of the within-cluster correlation when the number of clusters is known, without even needing an estimate of the within-cluster correlation. This is a surprising discovery as it contradicts the robust learning theory which necessitates an upper bound of the correlation for optimal solution effectiveness. The new results are further supported by an algorithm that can effectively estimate the robust risk without knowledge of the within-cluster correlation when the number of clusters is known, and can even effectively learn the robust risk when the number of clusters is unknown by averaging the robust risk over different assumed cluster sizes.

Let G be a countable abelian group, denoting upper banach density by $\rho^+$, and let $x$ and $y$ be nonempty subsets of G. The authors prove that if $\rho^+ \{nx + y\} = 1$ holds for every positive integer n, then it also holds for all subsets y of G. This generalizes a 2006 result by Bergelson, Furstenberg, and Weiss obtained for integers. Furthermore, it is shown that if $\rho^+ \{nx + y\} = 1$ holds for some subset y of G and for all but a finite number of n, then it must also hold for all subset combinations.

A crucial requirement for numerous transportation systems is the simultaneous management of route optimization and time scheduling. Although these problems have received considerable attention, most existing solutions rely on origin-destination information and ignore static road information. In contrast, real-world transportation services often come with these constraints. A proposed method in this paper makes full use of road information to boost computational efficiency. The method is based on an annealing algorithm with a modified criterion, known as the road-aware criterion, to ensure diversification. Empirical evidence demonstrates that the road-aware global criterion results in significantly faster convergence compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, incorporation of road information significantly accelerates the optimization process.

Current multi-modal learning architectures, relying solely on data-driven methods, often struggle with robustness when faced with varying modal and task combinations. To address this limitation, we introduce Knowledge Graph Augmented Multi-Modal Learning (KGMML), a novel approach that incorporates a knowledge graph to specify modal relationships and assign learning tasks. By leveraging a graph-based model, KGMML assigns edges to models, enabling inter-modal and task-related interactions. This mechanism enhances model flexibility and learns to operate across different modalities and tasks. As a generalizable framework, KGMML is versatile and compatible with various existing multi-modal learning architectures, demonstrating this flexibility on multiple benchmark datasets.

In recent years, deep learning models have gained significant traction in
medical image analysis, with many demonstrating superior performance
comparative to traditional approaches. Nonetheless, a great deal of expertise and
time is still required to label datasets for training these models. In this study,
we investigate whether unsupervised learning methods can effectively reduce
dependence on expert input. By employing a variational autoencoder and
autoencoder designs, we compare their performance against supervised
convolutional neural network models in predicting brain image features and
tracking Alzheimer's disease progression from a of 1524 MRI images. Our results
reveal that unsupervised learning methods hold promise for expert validation instead
of automated diagnosis, while variational autoencoder-based designs offer new
paths for disease progression prediction.

A key issue with delayed gradient methods like SGD is their slow response to recent data patterns due to lingering effects from past errors. The Backward Dropping Algorithm was developed to mitigate this limitation by effectively erasing past error contributions. Building upon this concept, we introduce a new method, BDA-ADAM, which builds on top of the ADAM algorithm by incorporating the error dropping mechanism. Theoretical and experimental analyses demonstrate that BDA-ADAM significantly enhances delayed gradient methods by rapidly converging to the optimal solution for non-stationary data patterns.

Our theoretical analysis focuses on the relationship between spin-orbit coupling and the Mott transition in the Hubbard model with carrier doping, with an intrinsic spin-orbit coupling present in the lattice.  By comparing the total energy of doped Hubbard models with and without spin-orbit coupling on lattice and dynamical clusters, we found the spin-orbit coupling enhances the Mott transition occurs at a higher value of on-site correlation.  Moreover, carrier doping shifts the Mott transition point towards higher doping levels when spin-orbit coupling is present, and the transition is shifted towards higher doping on the spin-free Hubbard model.  Both the inclusion of spin-orbit coupling and carrier doping lead to a spike in a spectral weight signal at the Doppler limit, but the spin-orbit coupling enhances this signal with smaller doping.  To gain insight into the underlying physics, we applied variational and exact diagonalization of two-site and four-site models with spin-orbit coupling, revealing the Mott transition is driven by competition between the spin-orbit coupling and the kinetic effect of carrier doping that overcomes the correlation-induced effective field.  Carrier doping amplifies the spin-orbit coupling in the system.  Our results suggest that spin-orbit coupling and carrier doping are complementary tools for engineering correlated materials, with potential implications for the vast array of materials with intrinsic spin-orbit coupling.

The interaction between dark matter and the Higgs field has significant implications for the early Universe, leading to an overproduction of dark matter if their coupling remains strong. In a specific theoretical framework involving a extended Higgs sector, this overproduction can be avoided by leveraging the dynamics between the Higgs and other scalar fields, allowing for variable speed of dark matter particles during early cosmic epochs. In this context, we examine the lightest neutral scalar in this theoretical framework, which can be produced via the process of dark matter + Higgs → dark matter + scalar, and the associated constraint from LHC data is also investigated. Moreover, the behavior of the scalar in question is analyzed in the context of the early Universe, with the aid of Boltzmann equations, which reveal a scenario in which this scalar contributes to an endogenous source of dark matter. Ultimately, our findings suggest that the dynamics between the Higgs and dark matter are intertwined with the early Universe, leading to the production of the lightest neutral scalar in question. In addition to this, we examine a theoretical model, which explains a dark matter mass of approximately 10 TeV. Specifically, this theoretical model, which is denoted as DM-S, postulates the presence of four scalar fields: two standard and two non-standard, with the standard scalars interacting with dark matter through a weakly suppressed coupling, and the non-standard scalars offering a pathway for dark matter to radiatively acquire mass. As black-box algorithms become more widely used in medical image processing, there is growing concern over their transparency. [J] proposes an innovative approach that incorporates conformal prediction to provide accurate uncertainty estimates for these models. This method initially creates predictions with guaranteed confidence intervals for input samples. Subsequently, the conformal prediction method is modified to generate such estimates by transforming the problem into a constraint optimization problem. To address issues related to data complexity, the proposed solution introduces a feature selection technique that optimizes predictive confidence intervals. This method is then demonstrated using popular medical image datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed technique in striking a balance between confidence and accuracy.

The RBB-NA algorithm employs a novel rotor-based approach to analyze distorted base pairs in nucleic acids, modifying traditional NA simulation methods to study biological processes that involve large conformational shifts. RBB-NA utilizes a reduced model of sugar-board combinations tied to rotating axes, contributing to a better comprehension of DNA and RNA structural changes. By its design, the algorithm is particularly effective in modeling DNA, but recent experiments demonstrate its potential for applying to RNA, specifically in modeling the open state of dA.C dG mispairing. However, validating the RBB-NA's relevance to RNA, especially RNA-protein complex structures, is necessary to confidently use it as a tool for scientific research. Here, comparative studies of DNA are used to establish trust in the algorithm, followed by its application to complex RNA structures to demonstrate validity. Ultimately, this approach may be used in reverse to provide new insights into RNA structure and the mechanisms behind mispairing at specific, sequential points on the DNA double helix.

This paper presents two new variants of adaptive non-uniform vector ANS, specifically designed to speed up the process of dividing integers with fixed accuracy in mind. The first variant achieves this by performing integer division in parallel with the encoding process of a floating point number, minimizing unnecessary bits and resulting in a compact representation of integers. The second variant builds upon range ANS by incorporating this optimized integer division technique, resulting in a modified range ANS encoding approach. Both methods are shown to maintain error bounds similar to floating point representation, with the new variants being more efficient in terms of bit usage in various test scenarios.

The observation of concrete in various stages of deterioration is carried out using dielectric sensing, a method that tracks dielectric properties in the material. Given its utility in multiple applications, dielectric sensing has been developed for both diagnostic purposes and to guide predictive maintenance. Although influential deep learning algorithms have been employed in recent studies, they have been used primarily for diagnostic purposes. In this work, a dielectric sensor's performance is evaluated by comparing the performance of three cutting-edge classification algorithms - Support Vector Machine, Random Forest, and XGBoost - when applied to pre-processed datasets created using the Fast Fourier Transform. These algorithms demonstrate strong results in both cases, with SVM and Random Forest exhibiting comparable performance when training and validation accuracy were considered, while XGBoost showed better performance when validation accuracy was examined. Consequently, it's suggested that these classification models be used in applications where predictive maintenance is necessary. Furthermore, it's also recommended that pre-processing data with the FFT before feeding the data to the machine learning algorithms enhance their performance.

The existence of heavy-heavy hadronic molecules, comprising two heavy components, is generally considered plausible. In this study, we broaden the scope to investigate the formation of light-light hadronic molecules, comprising two light components. Utilizing the formaldehyde and hydrogen molecular bond frameworks, we introduce a novel technique for searching experimentally relevant light-light molecular diplotons. Subsequently, based on perturbative quark-antiquark dynamics, we assess the feasibility of constructing bound states from light mesons and baryons. Our predictions for the mass spectra of the $S$-wave light-light hadronic molecules are presented.

The widespread adoption of unmanned aerial vehicles, or drones, in military operations has sparked debate over the ethics of remote-controlled warfare. Furthermore, technological advancements have enabled the development of swarming algorithms, allowing multiple drones to operate together, either autonomously or under central command. As a result, there is a growing concern that swarming algorithms could be exploited to launch "robotic terrorism" attacks, making it difficult to hold accountable those who control the drones. Through an analysis of existing literature and expert assessments, our research explores the global distribution of unmanned aerial vehicle capabilities, with the United States and Israel emerging as leaders in military drone development and swarming technology. Our findings indicate that, while swarming vulnerabilities exist in nearly every country's drone systems, countries are generally hesitant to disclose this information. Ultimately, our research aims to understand the gaps in existing literature and identify areas for further investigation into this critical issue.

A straightforward partial differential equation formulation resolves the central issue surrounding the CMB's spatial variation, namely, the ambiguity in choosing a reference epoch for z_f and the associated computational challenges. This ambiguity is crucial since the choice of $z_{f}$ affects computational precision; in particular, $z_{f} = 2.3$ is relevant to cosmological inferences at high precision. We integrate partial differential equation methods to extract information on $f_{\sigma_8}$ at $z=0$ from combined Planck data, optical surveys, and $H_0$ data, employing a Bayesian approach to model system parameters. We demonstrate that partial differential equation techniques seamlessly produce smooth solutions for $f_{\sigma_8}$ and accurately model Gaussian system noise. Moreover, partial differential equation methods outperform traditional approaches based on Taylor expansion by increasing precision by about $\sim 10^3$ and $\sim 10^2$ respectively. This partial differential equation framework's enhanced precision, particularly in modeling accuracy, not the noise, contributes to the main difference in precision in modeling $f_{\sigma_8}$ errors achieved.

An innovative concept developed by the IFUSM TM110 Cavity Project involves integrating a TM110 deflecting mode cavity within a bender arch framework to address limitations of traditional matching bellows restricting beam manipulation capabilities. The IFUSM TM110 cavity leverages its natural modes to tailor the matching process, enhance its mechanical robustness, and reduce requirements on downstream equipment such as beam position monitors and steering dipoles. The project undertakes a thorough investigation into numerical simulations, physical modeling, and experiments to optimize the TM110 cavity's design, which is then compared to an alternative elliptical matching section proposed in a different study.

Predicting human paths during crowd events is crucial for developing crowd simulation models with realistic behavior. Previous research, which our approach surpasses, included limitations such as: 1) they used simple models that failed to capture crowd behavior, 2) they relied on limited datasets, 3) they did not generalize well to new scenarios, and 4) they did not account for the uncertainty of new data. To overcome these issues, we present a Bayesian deep learning framework for predicting pedestrian paths during crowd events. This approach, which uses a Gaussian process to account for uncertainty in new data, enables the construction of a continuous crowd model from discrete data points. To assess the effectiveness of our method, we used the TrailNet dataset, which is more comprehensive than existing pedestrian datasets. Compared to previous research, our approach is more effective and generalizes well to new scenarios. To facilitate the development of crowd simulation models, we make the TrailNet dataset and our approach publicly available.

A statistical analysis of Boltzmann machine network dynamics reveals that its complexity grows with the number of neurons, time steps, and relevant parameters, suggesting an information-theoretic approach to studying critical phenomena. This approach can be applied to various machine learning algorithms to classify critical behavior. By applying the approach to a physical system, researchers can predict scaling relationships between physical characteristics and the system's architecture. The resulting scaling relations may facilitate a physical understanding of deep learning algorithms, including relationships between time (or iteration) and spatial dimensions, as well as connections between information and thermodynamic potentials. Ultimately, this approach may shed light on the physical nature of deep learning.

A swarm of robots working together to pick seeds from a field is an effective way to utilize multiple robots collaborating on a task. However, if the robots are too close to each other, they can interfere with each other's ability to pick seeds. By adjusting the distance between the robots, they can work at optimal capacity, maximizing their efficiency. This optimal distance, known as the "swarm radius," varies depending on the orientation of the robots in the field and should be regularly readjusted by the robots to ensure the best possible efficiency. A new control system has been developed that enables a swarm of robots to maintain an optimal spacing, based on the idea that each robot's efficiency is affected by its proximity to neighboring robots. By attributing this effect to the robot's rear, the swarm is able to maintain a consistent spacing, even when the "swarm radius" changes. A real-world experiment demonstrated the effectiveness of this control system in keeping the robots at the optimal distance.

The analysis of blood test results is a complex and time-consuming process requiring
the expertise of highly qualified healthcare professionals. Given its vital importance
to both patients and healthcare systems, efficiently analyzing blood tests is crucial.
Although automated systems can accurately analyze a significant portion of test results,
a second review by a healthcare professional is typically required to verify the findings.
In this study, we introduce a fully automated system for verifying the presence or quantity
of specific substances in blood tests, utilizing a compact net architecture. Our approach
involves three key components: (a) extracting relevant information from images of the tests, (b)
generating a list of potential substances based on patient data and (b) classifying substances
in the list as present or absent in the tested sample. Our system consists of a compact neural
network designed specifically for verifying blood test substances and a lightweight patient data parser.
We evaluated our system on 5953 patient data and achieved an average classification accuracy of 93%, 
both for quantity and presence/absence classification. Our experimental results demonstrate that
our system can reliably support fully automated blood tests.

A variational approach is approximated for the adiabatic gauge potential, with its variational parameters determined by minimizing the norm of commutators within a nested Lie algebra, leveraging the underlying mathematics of noncommutative differential forms and Lie algebra cohomology. The approximation accuracy is quantified by minimizing the norms of these commutators, revealing a relationship between variational parameters and the nested commutators' squared Frobenius norms. This variational method is validated for the SU(2) Lie algebra, specifically for its irreducible representations. While initially developed for adiabatic gauge theory, this approximation strategy is versatile and can be applied to other areas, as demonstrated by its previous use in a different context.

A phenomenon called chromatic aberration occurs when a lens separates white light into its color components, causing straight lines to appear curved due to differential refraction. Although this effect is obvious when viewing through a lens, its image-forming properties are less well-known. Our study experimentally investigated this aspect and found that a plane glass surface induces similar angle deviations as a lens, but with opposite curvature. Furthermore, we discovered that this effect has a significant impact on computer-generated holograms. To quantify this effect, we utilized the variations in hologram wavelength during image formation and found that it results in differential refraction. Our analysis revealed that this effect causes hologram curvature, leading to line deviations. Notably, we found that this effect is most pronounced for colors with the greatest wavelength disparities, such as red and violet, resulting in image curvature as depth perception. Conversely, green light, with its intermediate wavelength, experiences minimal curvature, making it the preferred choice for color grading applications.

The focus is on multiple mathematical series, initially developed by L. Fox and D. C. Spencer, and R. P. Levey, which relate to $C^{\omega}$ functions, particularly their potential convergence when series terms involve $C^{\omega}$ functions as coefficients. It is proven that these series converge under relaxed conditions, specified in terms of the Weierstrass kernel, even when infinite, provided certain criteria are met. This condition utilizes the concept of $\mathcal{C}^{\omega}$-Cauchy net, which can be thought of as a generalization of conventional $\mathcal{C}^{k}$-Cauchy nets. This study further explores the relationship between the Weierstrass kernel and the convergence of these series.

A closed surface $M$ with non-zero Euler characteristic, possessing an upper curvature bound, is considered. It is demonstrated that if the scalar curvature satisfies the inequality $\frac{c^2}{u^2} \geq k \geq -\frac{c^2}{n^2}$, where $c$ is a constant under the constraint $c<n$, then $M$ is conformally equivalent to the 2-sphere if and only if it is remotely isomorphic to the 2-sphere. When the constraint is removed, it is shown that if the curvature is positive or zero and the scalar curvature is negative with an absolute value less than $\frac{4n^2}{n-2}$, then $M$ is conformally equivalent to the 2-sphere if and only it is remotely isomorphic to the 2-sphere. This work generalizes the findings of Gaida's theorem. Furthermore, a complete classification has been achieved for the surfaces with an upper curvature bound that are conformally flat and contain a conformal field of 2-sphere, along with the identification of the complete set of axially symmetric surfaces with an upper curvature bound that are conformally equivalent to the 2-sphere.

A cutting-edge photon source was developed by integrating an experimental line from a laser-wakefield accelerator into the CEA's PHOTON facility. The custom-made photon beamline was designed to deliver up to 10 MeV photon beams of high brilliance and low background noise, making it an ideal platform for conducting innovative physics research. The facility's first experiment, the 'MENEX' investigation, is specifically utilizing this innovative beamline to explore the potential to significantly increase the detection rate of neutron decay experiments when compared to conventional methods.

In the IM Brans-Dicke model with a softly broken $Z_2$ symmetry in the Higgs sector, the mixing between $h$ and $H$ Higgs bosons occurs. As these bosons couple to $ZZ$, $Z\gamma\gamma$, and $\gamma\gamma$ respectively, the mixing also affects their coupling ratios as the Higgs sector undergoes non-minimal evolution. Notably, the coupling of the lightest $h$ boson to photons can be interpreted through the $Z$ boson's $\gamma\gamma$ coupling in the Standard Model (SM), thus restricting the degree to which $Z_2$ symmetry is broken. Additionally, the mixing leads to $h$-boson decay into photons, which has been observed by the LHC. Consequently, the mixing influences $h$-boson production cross-sections through $ZZ$, $Z$-jet, and $b\bar{b}$ processes. As these processes also involve $H$ production for various choices of the soft breaking parameter $s$, the total production of both $h$ and $H$ particles depends on these choices and are studied here for various scenarios.

We introduce a novel approach to solve the data exchange problem using a limited number of global conditions known as key covered conditions. A key covered condition is applied to a tuple once a specific primary key is established for it. Our solution has two main aspects, one is to ensure the local consistency of the solution using a general method and the other is to speed up the solution using a specific technique called source-to-target partial order flattening. It is demonstrated that a universal solution with key covered conditions exists only if a consistent solution with key covered conditions also exists. Moreover, if a consistent solution with key covered conditions exists, then it can specify the required universal solution with key covered conditions uniquely. Several interesting observations about the impact of key covered conditions on the existence and consistency of universal solutions are noted. These conditions ensure the existence of a universal solution, if it exists, to key covered conditions, as well as the number of global conditions required to guarantee the existence and consistency of a universal solution with key covered conditions is bounded by the square of the number of key covered conditions applied to a dataset. If the data sources have a finite number of global conditions, then a consistent solution with key covered conditions can be computed in at most two iterations of the iterated unfolding technique. It can be shown that using key covered conditions, a context-dependent recursive data exchange example serves as a counterexample to several previous results about the consistency and existence of universal solutions, as it fails to satisfy several conditions that previously guaranteed the consistency and existence

Scientists using various computational tools like Python, MatLab, and IDL to
analyze data often encounter difficulties with different complex data formats.
To address these issues, a unified data access approach is suggested, allowing
these tools to work in harmony. A proposed solution, the SOAP framework, enables
uniform retrieval of scientific data by utilizing Universal Description, Discovery,
and Integration (UDI) identifiers. Additionally, a new Python package, pyStoNED,
was developed to facilitate communication with multivariate regression libraries
and is proposed as a potential member of the SOAP community.

We examine the constraints on light scalar particles and how they impact the dark matter sector in a type-II two-Higgs doublet model. The Dark Matter Direct Detection experiments have imposed the hardsiest limitations on the dark matter-Yukawa interaction, especially at the High Luminosity phase of the LHC. Using beta decay of neutron experiments and considering a single scalar particle, we find that future limits on the coupling between the dark matter and scalar particles will be comparable to those obtained at the LHC. For a massless dark matter particle, current and future limits on the coupling between the dark matter and scalar particles will be comparable, while the coupling limits will be softer at LUXe3. Comparing the dark matter coupling to a scalar particle versus a gauge boson shows that future limits on the coupling to a scalar particle will be softer than that to a W boson.

This paper presents FPIO, a novel few-shot parsing model that achieves exceptional adaptability with minimal training. FPIO capitalizes on the power of transformers to efficiently process data, incorporating an object-level attention mechanism that generates query vectors in conjunction with a classification head's token-level attention, effectively identifying relevant semantic objects and their distinct constituents within target datasets. Through an innovative approach, FPIO adapts existing pre-trained models with user-defined object labels, automatically assigning corresponding labels to hidden tree structures. When tested with limited annotations, the results demonstrate FPIO outperforms previous few-shot parsing models by a substantial margin. Notably, FPIO parses new languages with nearly perfect accuracy using just five examples, achieving a score of 84.3%.

This study investigates the adaptability of speech recognition models to novel topics and speaker dialects, utilizing a diverse range of data. We reveal the effectiveness of data diversity in enhancing model resilience on unseen subjects, rather than incorporating additional examples. Notably, our experiment demonstrates that a model trained on data with high speaker diversity can also achieve top-notch performance on topic shifts, thereby establishing a connection between initial training data and a model's versatile capabilities. In addition to theoretical findings, we also present practical solutions to augment data scarcity limitations, proposing a simple, effective approach that outperforms multiple benchmark strategies in single-topic and multi-topic scenarios.

A study was conducted to examine the binary system identified as HEI~COP 3534 using photometry and radial velocity data. The light curve analysis favored a semi-detached binary system over an eclipsing binary. A 0.13 day orbital period, typical of Be-type stars, was observed, which distinguished this system from normal B-type stars. A significant radial velocity amplitude of 163.5 km/s, consistent with Be-type stars, was also found. A spectroscopic classification of the Be-type star led to a derived mass ratio of 0.53 and accretion mass of 3.2 x 10^-14 M_sun. A mass transfer rate of 1.2 to 2.4 x 10^-10 M_sun/year through the Roche lobe was estimated. Aoretical models of the Be-type star indicated a stellar mass of 7 to 10 M_sun, a stellar radius of 6 to 7 R_sun, a surface temperature of 10,500 K, and a luminosity of 1.1 to 1.4 times the luminosity of a standard B-type star of the same mass. A significant variability was found in the radial velocity of the system, which could be influenced by wind phases, a binary component, a companion mass greater than 1.5 M_sun, or a companion mass less than 1.2 M_sun. A significant variability was found in the radial velocity of the Be-type star

We aim to reduce the reliance of Image Text Navigation (ITN) models on in-domain training data by proposing a new data augmentation technique that can be used with off-domain and fine-tuning stages of training. While existing ITN models rely on ground truth image and text embeddings, our method generates alternative representations through off-domain image and text embeddings, thereby increasing the model's regional generalization capability. Experimental results indicate that our method surpasses previous data augmentation techniques and enhances the regional generalization performance of ITN models. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method, when combined with Text Transfer, results in robust regional generalization on ITN models even when trained on a completely unrelated dataset, such as COCO, and then fine-tuned on Novel Object 3D (NO3D). Notably, our method performs competitively with Text Transfer + Off-Domain Image-Text Mining (OIM) on NO3D, suggesting that ITN regional generalization can largely be achieved through off-domain image learning.

The purpose of this study is to provide a rigorous proof of a Faber-Krahn type inequality for the first eigenvalue of the Hermite operator in the Euclidean space. For the first eigenvalue of the Dirichlet Laplacian, the optimality of a ball's geometric configuration has been proven by Faber and Krahn in 1928. Building upon their work, this investigation demonstrates the same principle of optimality for the first eigenvalue of the polyharmonic operator in the Euclidean space. Contrary to the limitations imposed by classical methods that require lowering dimensions, this matter is resolved by presenting a general proof that raises dimensions. Moreover, this proof involves presenting a suitable counterexample for the second eigenvalue, challenging the extension of this theorem to higher eigenvalues.

Deep neural networks achieve impressive results but lack clarity in their decision-making processes. Researchers have developed neural tangent kernels as a compromise, allowing models to be more interpretable by drawing parallels with kernel methods. However, adopting NTKs comes with its own set of difficulties. To address this, we explored whether training only the trainable layers of an NTK, leaving the rest constant, could still serve as a suitable approximation. To our surprise, this approach proved to be a highly accurate model, achieving comparable results to incorporating an NTK into the network. Not only does this method uphold the model's interpretability, but it also offers significant enhancements to training stability and speed. We tested this approach on a range of datasets and tasks and found it to be a winning combination in many cases.

The extended Hatano-Nelson chain, made up of units with intrinsic decay, is studied when in a strong disorder setting with both real and complex coupling values. It is noted that while the disorder often leads to localized states, it doesn't always, and there's a band where localized and delocalized states coexist. It's in this area that the strength of coupling between units displays a notable change, resembling the behavior of a metal transitioning into a insulator, known as the skin effect. It's observed that the size of this effect, or the size of the outer part of the energy distribution, is directly correlated with the strength of the extra decay that occurs within each unit. It's seen that this effect can be either symmetrical or asymmetrical, depending on whether the decay is happening symmetrically or not, and there's a formula that can be used to calculate the size of this effect, or the size of the outer part of the energy distribution, in terms of the strength of the extra decay that occurs within each unit. It's observed that these effects can be seen in a physical model that involves two coupled oscillators that have complex coupling values. It's concluded that both intrinsic and external decay play a role in the behavior of these types of chains.

When creating synthetic speech for a female voice, the decision is often made to combine multiple vocal features in an attempt to convey a specific level of competence. It has been observed that combining these features in a convex manner leads to their increased interpretation in terms of competence, but the impact of this effect on acceptable competence levels is not well understood. A study was conducted which included a female speech synthesizer with a varied range of competence settings, and a group of listeners were asked to evaluate recordings made with differing competence settings in isolation, together, and with added modulation. The results of this study revealed that the effect of combining competence settings was not solely due to the summing of the recordings, as evident from the crowd's evaluations, which also showed that interactions between settings were considered relevant by the listeners. Consequently, it has been suggested that using a linear combination of competence settings to generate synthetic speech may not always be the most effective approach, and that a more tailored method that takes into account the potential interactions between the various vocal features may be necessary to produce a natural level of competence in synthetic speech.

A new theoretical model suggests that the instability in certain dark matter theories can be translated into stability by utilizing an $SU(3)$ gauge group for a hypothetical dark sector. This sector contains three heavy dark matter particles that exceed the mass of the Higgs boson. Additionally, the model includes three mass-generated bosons that mimic fermions in a magnetic monopole and fermion model, first introduced by 't Hooft. This sector's interaction with regular matter is minimal, which makes it possible according to current scientific observations.

This study investigates how a fundamental constant called the minimal length parameter affects the energy levels and transition probabilities of triaxial nuclei. To this end, we use a Hamiltonian with minimal length and apply the WKBT method to find the approximate wave functions of the nuclear states. The results show that as the minimal length parameter increases, the energy levels of triaxial nuclei decrease, with a greater rate of decrease observed for $2\gamma$ states, and superdeformed and $4^+$ rotational state energies. In contrast, the transition probabilities show a tendency to increase with elevated minimal length parameter values.

This article confirms the feasibility of all quaternary Golay complementary array pairs of lengths 23^4 and 24^4, and provides the definitions for feasible and strongly feasible quaternary Golay complementary arrays, along with a characterization of feasible quaternary Golay complementary array pairs based on their component PC arrays.

Although change detection techniques have made significant advancements, many existing methods still rely on extensive labeled data. In the field of Object-Oriented Imaging, this remains a critical challenge for implementing these techniques. A new approach called the Random Forest Unknown-Known Editor (RAKE) has been developed for unsupervised change detection, enabling the identification of changes within an image without requiring training datasets. Preliminary experiments demonstrate that RAKE performs comparably to supervised methods, while significantly reducing data requirements. Further experiments aim to investigate any potential biases in RAKE's outcomes and evaluate its effectiveness in detecting subtle changes over time.

Utilizing MD simulations and NMR experiments, we have investigated how density is affected by the complexity of non-associating molecular fluids. The viscosity data collected from MD simulations is compared to the predictions made by various models, revealing that these models significantly overestimate the impact of density on viscosity when it increases. In contrast, the NMR experiments reveal a more nuanced relationship between density and complexity, with increased density leading to greater molecular interaction and elevated complex presence. The discrepancy between the MD and NMR findings is attributed to the inherent limitations of the MD model, which inaccurately captures density fluctuations in liquids by underrepresenting the corresponding state. By applying the hard-sphere viscosity model to the MD data, we have been able to reconcile the results with the NMR findings, illustrating that this model accurately accounts for the density's influence on viscosity when an appropriate state-bias is applied. In addition, we have observed a linear correlation between the viscosity contribution from complexes and their formation rate constant, supporting the earlier observation that complex formation is rate-limited. The complexity's role in viscosity can thus be described by the equilibrium ViscoComplex criterion, which compares the complex formation and dissociation rates to determine the viscosity contribution.

A time-dependent cosmological model is proposed which, when analyzed over a specific time period, exhibits behaviors characteristic of both Lambda CDM and inflation. When considered in relation to GRW models of wave-particle duality, our model's Lambda CDM phase aligns with the non-selective collapse of a quantum cosmology field, which in turn gives rise to the periodic cosmology described here. The need for a subsequent inflationary phase in our model stems from a quantum cosmology field's inherent instability. The model suggests a quantum cosmology field could serve as an effective dark energy source, which, when contrasted with a certain type of dark energy in DE-LSS models, shares certain similarities, although our model also displays notable differences. The concept of measurement independence in quantum theories is widely discussed, yet its meaning remains ambiguous. Many attribute nonlocality to violations of Bell's theorem, while others associate it with entanglement. However, 1st-order correlations, which include Bell's theorem, also reveal much about local causality. To resolve this, we propose a new framework, which contrasts nonlocality and nonantilocality, defining the latter as deviations from independent measurements affecting distinct variables. Through this distinction, we demonstrate that nonantilocality naturally arises from quantum causality, entanglement, and even local causality constraints, thus providing a comprehensive explanation for all three. Moreover, we show that quantum theories, which are comprised of both nonlocal and nonantilocal theories, are uniquely defined by the principle of 3rd-party quantum causality, which is ultimately linked to quantum graphs. Consequently, we propose that quantum graphs offer a unified explanation for Bell's theorem, the quantum causal structure of Alice's spin, and the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen paradox.

This paper presents a comprehensive survey of recent advancements in the field of Compact Neural Networks (CNNs), which significantly reduce memory and computation requirements by limiting the size and complexity of neural models. The survey focuses on two primary aspects: decreasing model size and complexity through data and representation techniques, and increasing efficiency by exploiting hardware features and adopting novel architectures. The assessment of 16 frameworks serves as a practical guideline for choosing the best toolset for implementing CNNs on devices such as voice assistants, fitness trackers, and medical devices. The survey provides recommendations on the most suitable CNN types, processing strategies, activation functions, optimization methods, and auto-generation approaches to facilitate successful deployment of CNNs on embedded devices.

A novel cluster expansion framework is presented for the dimer model on isorial graphs, offering a detailed analysis of the dimer model's properties. By applying a specific matching algorithm for cluster terms, a refined expansion is created which eliminates cluster overlaps. This advanced analysis enables the identification of a cluster term that is universally present and well-defined. Consequently, a precise, single-term cluster expansion is derived for the dimer model. Several conditions for the cluster expansion converge, providing explicit formulas in various situations. Club domains and dual graphs associated with the dimer model are also introduced and explored.

For multivariate response regression analysis, the Group Lasso method offers a type that can select blocks or groups of variables, which is particularly suitable for handling continuous or categorical data. In cases where responses are correlated, the Group Lasso can identify the common sets of active variables across multiple responses, which is not achievable with conventional variable selection techniques. Building upon the original Lasso algorithm of Friedman et al., this paper proposes a specialized solver for the Group Lasso, formulated as a convex optimization problem with a sparsity constraint in a particular Banach space. These theoretical advancements can be applied to three different formulations of the Group Lasso, two of which are based on the 'one-the-best' transformation of Friedman et al., and the third using the weighted average of grouped $\ell_1$ norms from Zhao et al. The proposed algorithm is then adapted for penalized estimation of grouped regression, which includes non-differentiable objective functions and grouped $\ell_1$ Lasso. The estimation efficiency of the proposed algorithm is evaluated using simulated and real data examples from gene expression and brain cancer studies, demonstrating its effectiveness for both linear and logistic regression analyses.

T-Visor is a lightweight, portable virtual machine introduced in this paper.
It is designed to efficiently manage and utilize the last level cache,
providing a cache-friendly interface for guest applications and isolating
memory and scheduling risks. The visitormanager in T-Visor implements an
advanced scheduling framework, accommodating the varied real-time needs of
embedded systems. The framework synchronizes visitor and manager thread
interactions through a cache-friendly interface, and dynamically adjusts
thread scheduling, preempting and sleep operations, to optimize cache usage.
The study evaluates the T-Visor scheduling framework's performance under
real-world application benchmarks, and the experiment results show that T-Visor
delivers schedule-agnostic, predictable and high cache latency, making it
suitable for hard real-time systems.

A panoramic image composite captured by multiple cameras aligned from 2D or 2.5D world models often includes unwanted reflection or distortion flaws. To rectify this issue, a new method utilizes IMUs to track camera orientation and position with high accuracy. By integrating IMU data and refining it with image processing algorithms leveraging the Baeker-Keller algorithm and the direct linear transformation method, we've developed an efficient and effective process for correcting distortion in panoramic images. Unlike existing solutions, our approach doesn't require the precise synchronization of IMUs, making it practical for real-world applications. Moreover, this method remains adaptable even in the presence of camera movement constraints. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our approach successfully removes distortion and improves image clarity, while also estimating camera rotation and translation. Moreover, this algorithm can be optimized with fewer images captured than other methods, requiring only 3 to 4 pictures for correct alignment, thus making it more applicable in real-life scenarios.

In networks of oscillators displaying different levels of activity, either uniform or variable, certain configurations known as chimeras may occur. Research so far indicates that when in a chimeric state, some oscillators synchronize while others are independent, however this has primarily been observed in networks with homogeneous activity configurations. We have expanded on this by examining how the stability of chimeras is affected by heterogeneity within the network. Using an example of logistic maps in a complete graph, we found that increasing heterogeneity tends to enhance the stability of chimeras, contrary to what's typically observed. Furthermore, through an in-depth analysis, we have managed to create an equation which accurately predicts the conditions necessary for a stable chimeric state to occur.

It's been demonstrated that controllers learned through training in simulation, such as Q-learning, are robust when the simulation accurately models the system's noise dynamics. However, this may not be the case when the noise in the training simulation does not accurately reflect the noise in the real system. In this study, we address this issue by training a dynamic system model with a minimum likelihood noise floor, effectively preventing the training algorithm from optimizing away noise that could be detrimental in real-world scenarios. By enforcing this noise floor, the training process is forced to account for noise that is below the threshold, resulting in controllers that are robust when transferred to the testing stage, even when the noise in the real system is less than the threshold. Our method is validated through experimentation using the gazebo/mav platform, as well as through analytical evaluation in continuous systems modeled using smooth manifold dynamics, where we find that the introduced constraint is all that's needed to ensure the learned controller performs acceptably when noise levels are reduced.

It's a prevalent custom to denote the algebra obtained by taking linear combinations of paths within a quiver Q using a base field or ring R as P(Q,R). However, the definition can be expanded to cover "path algebras" in more complex scenarios. Drexel's study proposes a structural approach to matrix and tensor algebras as special cases of path algebras, utilizing modifications to matrices or tensors as equivalent to certain types of path expressions. This work develops further extensions, first by showing P(Q,R) also represents the algebra resulting from combining all possible matrix algebras based on subgraphs of P(Q,R), then by demonstrating a similar principle applies to tensor algebras. These findings can be used to establish a more streamlined interpretation of how P(Q,R) operates as a graded algebra. Additionally, P(Q,R) is shown to be the free graded algebra generated by matrix and tensor algebras based on subgraphs of P(Q,R).

Real-world applications of quantum error correction face significant challenges due to the extensive entanglement present in quantum systems. Addressing these challenges requires developing novel methods to capture the fundamental properties of entangled states, especially those that emerge at the boundary of entanglement. We investigate the reflected entanglement spectrum, a phenomenon arising from the application of a local projection tensor in the context of random tensor networks, and demonstrate its utility in describing local entanglement. By comparing the reflected spectrum with the typical R'enyi spectrum, we reveal the asymptotic equivalence of the two within the context of a specific projective layer. Moreover, our work demonstrates the existence of a family of free tensor networks characterized by a spectrum consisting of solely twos, thus enabling the construction of new entanglement measures. We leverage these measures to develop a set of local entanglement spectra capable of capturing the spectrum of a distant, entangled region without direct access to it. Specifically, for a ball-shaped region in a distance d, we show the asymptotic equivalence of the reflected spectrum, the typical R'enyi spectrum, and the spectrum of a free tensor network with a depth of log(d+1) + O(1).

This work develops a framework to estimate the probability of long-term persistence in complex dynamical systems, which are characterized by multiple stable equilibria and large, diverse initial conditions. Building on earlier analysis of probabilistic switching networks, the study generalizes these findings to a broader class of nonlinear systems subject to state-dependent modulation. The researchers provide specific guidelines for numerical model construction, while also offering numerical examples to demonstrate their approach's efficacy and outline key challenges for future investigation.

To analyze the structure of parameter space in family types of quadratic diffeomorphams, it's crucial to understand how periodic orbits contribute to this space, especially their effects on renormalization. As indicated by results from \cite{Kitaev2013}, the divergence of the itinerary set $\{i_{\alpha}^p\}_{\alpha\in I^+}$ for a given point $\alpha$ at the first iterate $p=1$ indicates the point's entry into a new resonance region. However, for most $p>1$, it's unclear how the itineraries $i_{\alpha}^{p+1}$ relate to those of $i_{\alpha}^p$, making it hard to predict when a point will transition into a new resonance. This study aims to resolve this issue by characterizing the points $\alpha$ for which the itineraries $i_{\alpha}^{p+1}$ and $i_{\alpha}^p$ are "convergent" or "repeating," especially for small values of $p=1,2$ and under specific conditions on the itineraries $i_{\alpha}^1$ and $\alpha$ related to "visits" to sites $\iota_0$ and $\iota_1$. As a result, we can specify the "visits" to sites $\iota_0$ and $\iota_1$ at the first iterate

Holonomy in gauge theory is well understood as a property of SU(N) and similar groups, but an equivalent effect in gravity has been elusive until now. Research suggests that gravity's holonomy is distinct from what is expected when applying gauge theory principles, especially when dealing with negative curvatures. In the presence of an Einstein-Hilbert term, a new understanding of holonomy is proposed, revealing it to be a SU(N) symmetry that is gauge equivalent but not identical.

For large values of $n$, the asymptotic behavior of the cumulative distribution functions of the variables $X_n/\sqrt{n}$, $X_n/n$, and $(X_n - \mu_n)/\sigma_n$ is similar to that of the corresponding variables $Z$, $aZ$, and $(a-1)Z$ for certain sequences $X_n$ and $\mu_n$ with zero mean, and $\sigma_n$ with positive variance, where $a>0$ and $Z$ is a standard normal variable.

The underlying process governing tunneling through the barrier is explained by two approaches - the classical tunneling time (CTT) and the actual tunneling time (ATT), with the latter more accurately capturing the phenomenon. Previous developments of ATT formulations have introduced inconsistencies and ambiguities in relation to spin fluctuations, especially in the context of ATT for interactions involving spin. This work presents a novel ATT formulation that rectifies these issues, demonstrating its applicability to various interaction types, including non-relativistic and relativistic interactions, as well as interactions involving spin. Utilizing the wave function, this newly introduced ATT can be calculated and provides consistent results, eliminating previous discrepancies. Its application to various potential barriers reveals a direct correlation between ATT, tunneling time, and barrier height/width, thereby validating its practicality and usefulness.

We've approached the challenge of extracting relativistic corrections to amplitudes involving P-wave charmonia mesons from data provided by LHCb. This involves utilising information on relativistic corrections to charm and charm-like beauty mesons as obtained from $\kappa$ and $\pi\pi$ processes, amplifying their magnitude due to the larger momentum values in J/psi decay processes. The resulting relativistic corrections to these P-wave amonium amplitudes are notably substantial, up to 20%, 30% and 40% for the H_c, H_cs and H_ct amplitudes respectively. This is notably larger than the 10% correction observed for S-wave states like D_Dbar or B_Bbar.

This study utilizes generalized Ramsey interferometry with Bose-Einstein condensates to determine the efficiency of mult-mode, multi-pulse Hadamard gates producing entangled states. By applying attractive interactions among atoms in the same mode and leveraging the quantum nonlinearity in these interactions, we analyze the limitations and optimal performance of these gates. Our research indicates that, contrary to linear gates, additional pulses increase entropy, reducing entanglement density in the system. However, in specific cases, these extra pulses ensure perfect formation of GHZ states regardless of noise levels. Moreover, we find that, contrary to linear gates, which fail due to thermal noise, our non-linear gates remain effective even in the presence of thermal fluctuations, generating states over the thermal noise limit. Finally, we find that, unlike linear gates, which fail due to decoherence from photon losses, our non-linear gates continue to produce entangled states even in the presence of decoherence from photon losses.

The Resolvent Partition Function, a key construct in spectroscopy, shares crucial aspects with the Fano resonance observed in various systems. A wavefunction description enabled the derivation of a determinant, a fundamental component of the Resolvent, using transfer matrix analysis and the Schrodinger equation. Observations indicate that the underlying mathematical structure of the Resolvent holds important non-unitary aspects that significantly impact its application in complex systems. Notably, in contrast to real-time scenarios where the Yang-Mills-Schwartz theory applies, our study in random matrix theory emphasizes the role of soft degradation in the emergence of non-unitary behaviors. Our analysis explicitly demonstrates how the multiple degeneracies in the calculated vacua contribute to the non-unitary nature of the Resolvent, a behavior distinct from the previously proposed Schwazian description. As such, our findings suggest that the existing Schwazian description requires refinement or alteration in the context of the Resolvent.

A conventional approach to training neural networks involves using supervised gradient-based methods. However, these methods can sometimes fall short, particularly in complex classification tasks. A novel solution to this problem is presented, involving an ensemble method that surpasses the performance of standard training methods. The proposed method, which is rooted in advanced training techniques for linear regression, effectively leverages an overcomplete neural network model to achieve exceptional classification results. The method's underlying theory and its practical applications in image classification and neural text analysis are discussed in detail.

Our study reveals a relationship between generalized connections and locally invariant generalized metrics, leading to a definition of parallel generalized fields. We demonstrate that Ricci flat generalized metrics can be produced from generalized Einstein metrics and, conversely, constant generalized curvature generalized metrics are Einstein. Additionally, we derive generalized fields equations from the generalized Einstein-Hilbert action, specifically focusing on surfaces where a particular gauge is applicable, yielding familiar equations such as the vanishing Riemann surface.

The term 'complete mapping' is used to describe a function that maps every element of the field $\mathbb{F}_{p^m}$ (with m greater than 1 and both p and m being prime numbers) to every element of the field $\mathbb{F}_q$ without repetition, to every element of the field $\mathbb{F}_{p^{mn}}$ (with m and p are both prime numbers) without restriction. Human visual inspection for intestinal parasites is widely regarded for its ease of use and effectiveness, although it's also known to have a relatively high error rate. The establishment of machine learning-based vision paradigms for intestinal parasite identification has recently brought about a level of objectivity in the diagnostic process. Despite this progress, the topic remains relatively under-researched and there is still a significant gap in knowledge about the subject. A thorough examination of existing studies on the subject was carried out in this context, which collected and synthesized data on the topics most relevant to intestinal parasite diagnosis, including the best machine learning algorithms, feature extraction techniques, data sets used, and evaluation metrics. The analysis of existing studies also covered potential future directions for further research. As a result, this paper aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of the art and provide valuable insights for researchers and practitioners in the field of intestinal parasite diagnosis.

This paper uses the variational iteration method to solve nonlinear integro-differential Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations under uncertain parameters. The method applies the initial condition in a corrective formula, generating successful successful successful successful successful successful successful successful successful with 100% success rate for 20 test problems. The average number of iterations needed to obtain an accurate result was determined to be 1.625, with an average convergence rate of 99.983%. The formula's applicability was extended to 6-dimensional spaces, and results for 20 test problems showed a high degree of accuracy.

Unstable quadcopter control often suffers from significant errors due to external factors, limited sensor capabilities, and system imperfections.  To counteract this issue, advanced techniques combining state estimation and feedback control have been developed but still face constraints.  This study introduces a new Genetic Filter that enhances robustness in quadcopter control by utilizing a neural network to generate reference commands with adaptive tracking performance.  The proposed Genetic Filter improves the state estimation process by optimizing the filter's coefficients through a search algorithm.  Successful simulation results validate the algorithm's effectiveness and demonstrate its ability to achieve robust adaptation in various challenging scenarios.

The CNM-INDIANA-BATES Collaboration accurately measured the pion-nucleon sigma term using pseudoscalar-pole sum rules and comprehensive pseudoscalar-pole sum rules covering both the second and third resonance regions. This was made possible through an analysis of existing pion-nucleon scattering cross-section data collected over nearly five decades. Our calculation of the sigma term is unaffected by uncertainties stemming from the sigma term's variability and the contributions of higher-resonance states. This research is significant as it addresses an enduring nuclear physics enigma, and the sigma term also bears importance in the study of lambda hypernuclei and strange hadron condensates in dense matter.

The CMS detector's two innermost layers were upgraded with a 2020 detector upgrade, which included two specialized detector layers covered in silicon. This upgrade was done to enhance the detector's ability to track particle trajectories in the detector. After the upgrade was installed and data collection began in 2017, tests were conducted on the new detector layers by analyzing data from proton-proton collisions at a high energy of 13 TeV. Analysis results showed that the new trajectories could be tracked with high precision, meeting or exceeding expectations for performance in several key areas. This improved tracking accuracy and identified new categories for making distinctions in physics analyses in regions where there is otherwise high momentum uncertainty, which was seen in experiments analyzing the production of J/psi particles and track-based measurements.

Using the XMM-COSINE survey's 106 square degrees of the cosmic epoch survey fields, we identified 509 separate X-ray sources stronger than 1 count per second. Our research details the initial findings regarding the 509 sources' optical properties. A highly accurate optical catalog produced by matching XMM-COSINE with SDSS DR12, was employed for the optical analysis of the 509 sources. In doing so, we successfully linked an optical counterpart to 463 sources, leaving 46 unsolved. A highly accurate classification of an optical AGN host galaxy was achieved for 217 sources, whereas 226, 16, and 10 sources were classified as type A, type B, and star, respectively, or type C (likely star or type C), consisting of 10 likely star and 10 likely type C. A comparison between the XMM-COSINE and SDSS optical redshifts, revealed that Type A AGN have a redshift precision of 6.6% in the z = 0-0.1 interval, 20.2% in the z = 0.1-0.6 interval, and 39.4% in the z = 0.6-1.0 interval. A highly accurate correlation existed between two different teams for the classification of the 217 sources, achieving precision of 92%, as well as between the two teams for host galaxy subtypes, achieving precision of 93%.
